Kuṟuntokai 130. Veḷḷi Vīti(yār): the confidante / SHE

lg.l: varuneṟi niṉaintu vāra leṉṟaluṅ
kāppiṭai yīṭṭiṟ kaiyaṟu kiḷaviyum
varuka veṉṟalum vāra leṉṟalum
paṭaittu moḻitaluṅ kuṭittiṟaṅ kūṟalu
marivaiyai yiṉṟiyā ṉaṟintē ṉeṉṟalō
ṭuriyaṉa kiḷanta piṟavun tokaii
varaivu kaṭāta lāku meṉmaṉār.
[The heroine] thinking of the path by which [the hero] comes and saying, ‘Do not come’;
the desolate speech [of the confidante] on account of [the heroine’s] being placed under guard;
[the confidante] saying [to the hero], ‘[You] ought to come’; [the confidante] saying [to the hero], ‘Do not come’;
[the confidante] speaking fabrications; [the confidante] speaking of the state of [their] family;
[the hero] saying, ‘Now I know [she is] a young woman’
– they say that [these] and other appropriate ones expressed, taken together,
are [the situations of] asking for marriage.

div.p: eṉpatu varaivu kaṭātal ām āṟuṇarttutaṉutaliṟṟu.
The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which asking for marriage occurs.

āṟu pārttuṟṟa vaccak kiḷaviyum varavu vilakkaluṅ kāppiṉ iraṅkiya kaiyaṟu kiḷaviyum iraviṉum pakaliṉum nī vā veṉṟalum vāral eṉṟalum paṭaittu moḻitaluṅ kuṭit tiṟaṅ kūṟalumāṉiṭa makaḷ ātal iṉṟaṟintēṉ eṉṟalum eṉa viṉṉa vellām varaivu kaṭātal eṉṟu colluvar pulavar eṉṟa vāṟu.

lg.l: āṟē yariya veṉṉā yāṟē
malkupuṉal parantu kalluyarn taṉavē
yiraviṉ varuvarnaṅ kātala
ruravēṉ ṟōḻiyā ṉuyirvāḻ vēṉē.

You do not sayCould eṉṉāy have a similar rhetorical flavour to a negative imperative – ‘O, do not say…!’? There are parallels in the Caṅkam corpus, where it seems to function as a participial noun (cf. Kali 39.10, 14, 18; Kali 48.12), but I see no reason why that would be more likely than the finite form here. that the way is difficult.ariya is understood here as an adjective, but could also be a pronominalised noun in the neuter plural: ‘there are dangerous things on the way’. On the way,

the swelling flood spreads and the rocks are tall.Is the idea that there are rocks that protrude from the ground and make walking painful? Or is this a result of the swelling waters? We have to understand a subject-changing viṉaiyeccam, as uyar-tal (‘to be tall/raised’) is intransitive and can only take kal (‘stone’) as a subject in this phrase – puṉal is a singular. The question becomes one of semantics: is the idea that there are rocks that protrude from the ground and make walking painful, or are they risen (i.e., carried) in the swelling waters? I understand the former. In parallels, this collocation of kal and uyar-tal appears multiple times. In all cases, it refers to tall rocks, or something tall and rocky (cf. KT 235.3, 275.1, Tiruneṭuntāṇṭakam 15.1).
Our lover will come in the night. I am not strong, O friend!

[How] will I live life?This understanding necessitates taking the particle -ē in vāḻvēṉ-ē as an interrogative. This is not the normal function at the end of a poem, but it is one of the accepted functions of the particle (see TC 259n).

div.p: eṉpatu āṟu pārttuṟṟa vaccak kiḷavi.
This is [the heroine’s] speech about [her] fear when thinking about [the hero’s] path.

lg.l: vārā tīmō cāra ṉāṭa
vuṟupuli koṉṟa ciṟukaṇ yāṉai
yāṟukaṭi koḷḷu maruñcura
mūṟu tuṭaiya tamiyai nīyē.
Please don’t come, O man from the land with mountainsides!

You, all alone, faceThis is not the most literal translation for the phrase ūṟutu uṭaiya. The idea is that he has an affliction waiting for him. This is a close but still idiomatic way to translate. an obstacle
– the difficult desert, where the way is guardedāṟu kaṭi koḷḷum arum curam literally translates to: ‘The difficult desert, where the way takes protection (of the elephant)’.

by small-eyed elephants that are killed by strong tigers.As in KT 88, this phrase – uṟu puli koṉṟa ciṟu kaṇ yāṉai – is unmarked for case, but here the word order suggests that it is the tigers that kill the elephants. Possibly this flips that image to reinforce the danger the hero would face on the way.

div.p: eṉpatu varavu vilakkiṟṟu.
This is [the confidante] having prevented [the hero’s] coming.

lg.l: yāyē tuyiṉmaṟan taṉaḷē yāyiṉu
nāyu mūru naṉituñ calavē
kāva lāḷa rataṉiṉun tuyilā
rāykatir matiyaniṉ ṟalarum
yāva tāṅko lēntiḻai nilaiyē.
Mother has forgotten sleep. On top of that,
the dogs and the village do not sleep at all.
And even more than that, the watchmen don’t sleep.

And the moon with beautiful rays is in constantniṉṟu is understood here as ‘continuing’, but one could also translate: ‘the moon stands [there] shining’. With the poem’s structure of escalating comparative clauses, the chosen translation seems more apt. bloom.
What will become of the girl with the eminent jewels?

div.p: eṉpatu kāppiṉ iraṅkik kaiyaṟu kiḷavi.

This is [the confidante’sThe situation is not entirely clear. It could be the heroine speaking, though if that were the case, it would be odd for her to refer to herself in the third person.] speech about [the heroine’s] overwhelming sadness, weeping because [she is under] guard.

lg.l: pakalē variṉu māṟṟāḷ pakaliṉ
ṟiraviṉ variṉu mannilai yiṉaḷē
viraicēr mārpa ceytiṟam viḷampē.

When you come onlyThis translates the emphatic particle -ē in pakalē. One could also understand a slightly different function, in which case: ‘in the middle of the day’. Considering pakal iṉṟu in the next line, the translation of ‘only’ is most convincing as it provides the clearest counterpart. in the day, she is inconsolable.
And when you come at night but not by day, that is also [the case].
O man with the fragrant chest, say what is to be done!

div.p: eṉpatu iraviṉum pakaliṉum nī vā veṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having said, ‘You come, either by day or night.’

lg.l: murukaṟ cevviyoṭu pakalvari ṉivvaḻi
viraviyaṟ kavvai yañcutu
miruḷvari ṉataṉiṉum peritañ cutumē.
When you come along this way in the day with the beautyOr simply ‘appearance’ for cevvi. of Murukaṉ,

we fear the scandal of our mixed nature.The semantics of viravu iyal kavvai are not clear. It could either refer to the scandal that concerns the hero and the heroine’s union, or a scandal that itself is of a mixed and thus varied nature (i.e., random unfocused gossip).
If you come at night, we fear even more than that.

div.p: eṉpatu iraviṉum pakaliṉum vāral eṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having said, ‘Do not come, either by day or night.’

lg.l: kaḻippūṅ kāṉa livvaḻi nerunal
vaḻippaṭarn tuṇṭōr tēreṉa
vaḻittu nōkkiṉa ḷemmaṉai peritē.
Yesterday, on this path through the backwaters and flowery seashore grove,
leaving on [its] way, there was this one chariot.

Thinking of it, our motheremmaṉai can be split in two ways and interpreted in three: em maṉai (‘our house’, ‘our mother’), or em aṉai (‘our mother’). Based on what we find in the IAC and PK source material, the likely meaning of the phrase is ‘our mother’. In both cases, the mother looks in anger at the confidante, signalling her knowledge of the affair. If one were to take it as ‘our house’, then the mother could be indicating her desire to confine the heroine by looking at the house where the heroine will be locked up. This reading would require supplying the mother as the subject of nōkkiṉaḷ (‘she looked’). Of the other two options, em maṉai as ‘our mother’ would require understanding a metonymy – the house refers to the mother as she keeps their home. This is not, however, a designation found for the mother, and other similar forms – pronominal derivations of maṉai – refer to the heroine, not the mother. The reading taken in the translation is also not without its own discomfort. aṉai is not a normal word for ‘mother’. One would have to understand it as a contracted form or variant spelling of aṉṉai/aṉṉāy. Such a spelling is not present in the Caṅkam corpus and is not recorded in lexica that I have seen, but we do find a parallel in the Vaiṣṇava corpus, in line 31 of the Ciṟiya Tirumatal. For more on this, see \S\ref{sec:other-influences} of the introduction. looked intently [at me].

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi paṭaittu moḻintatu.
This is the confidante having spoken fabrications.

lg.l: kaḻaikeḻu cilampi ṉaruvi yāṭu
maḻaimata yāṉaiyoṭu piṭikaṇ
ṭuḻaikeḻu nōkki yuṉṉiṉaḷ peritē.

Seeing the female elephant with its cloud-coloured male in rut,There are three different options for how to understand maḻai mata yāṉai. First option: as translated. Second option: ‘male elephant in rut under the rain’, where maḻai means ‘rain’. Third option: ‘male elephant with ichor raining [from it]’, where maḻai is understood as an attribute of the elephant’s musk.
playing under the waterfall on the mountainside full of bamboo,
she, with her doe-like glances, thought long and hard.

div.p: ituvum atu.

And this is that.Both this and the previous poem are spoken by the confidante to try and convince the hero to marry the heroine. She alludes to this in the first case by suggesting that his actions are becoming known, which he realises means marriage is the right course of action. In this poem, by relaying the heroine’s wistful encounter with a loving elephant-couple, the suggestion is that she longs for the same level of commitment from the hero.

lg.l: varaital vēṭṭaṉi rāyiṟ pativayi
ṉetirkoḷ cevviya remarē yivvayi
ṉaṟunutaṟ peruntōṭ pētaiyuñ
ciṟukuṭik kāṉavaṉ perumaṭa makaḷē.

If you desire marriage, our people are readyEither this is implying that they are now ready to accept his marriage proposal, and that this is the opportune time for him to approach them, or that they are good, upright people who are worthy of marrying into the hero’s lineage.

to welcome you to [our] abode.pati-um can either refer to an ‘abode’, or to a ‘husband’. Either work here, though I think the latter a more likely interpretation considering the following locative postposition – vayiṉ. Understanding ‘husband’, one might take vayiṉ as ‘in the place of’, so: ‘as a husband’.

Here, the foolish girlThe force of -um in pētaiyum is not obvious. In this translation, the daughter is, in addition to being her father’s daughter, also a girl like any other. ‘Still’ or ‘just’ are more natural translations in English, but that moves away from the prescribed meanings of the particle. with a fragrant forehead and large shoulders
is the greatly innocent daughter of the man of the forest from a small clan.

div.p: eṉpatu kuṭit tiṟaṅ kūṟiyatu.
This is [the confidante] talking about the state of [their] family.

lg.l: itaṟkoṇ ṭiṉiyān terintatu mēṉāḷ
matikkō ṭuriñcu mālvarai vāḻkkaik
kaṭavu ḷāka vallatu
maṭavaraṉ mātarai matittaṉṟō vilamē.
We have taken this in and now we understand it –
Until yesterday, we never thoughtLit.: ‘we were without any thought of’. Cf. NA 27, 193, and 239 for parallel constructions to matittaṉṟō ilamē. of the innocent woman
[as anything] other than as a god
living on the great mountain that touches the moon.

div.p: eṉpatu iṉṟaṟintēṉ eṉṟal. 19.
This is [the hero] saying, ‘Today, I knew [her].’

Cf. IA30.2: kāppuc ciṟaimikka kaiyaṟu kiḷavi
Cf. TP210n.5: kiḻavōṉ ṟaṉṉai vāra lenṟal
Cf. IA30.5: kiḻavōṉ ṟaṉṉai vāra lenṟal
Cf. IA12.8: paṭaittumoḻi kiḷavi

The situation for which the TP employs this phrase is slightly different, but as this is the only time in the TP where this phrase is used, it is reasonable to expect that this would have been known to the author of this text. In the TP it refers to the desolation of an intermediary arguing for the hero to be allowed home after an affair.
Cf. IA30.3: āṟupārt tuṟṟa vaccak kiḷavi
Cf. AV164.11: āṟupārt tuṟṟa vaccak kiḷavi
Cf. AV164.14: neṟivilakku vittal
Cf. AV164.13: taṉṉuṭ kaiyā ṟeytiṭu kiḷavi
Cf. TP207n.4: iraviṉum pakaliṉu nīvara veṉṟal
Cf. IA30.4: iraviṉum pakaliṉu nīvāru keṉṟal
Cf. AV166.6–8: pakalvaru vāṉai yiravuvaru keṉṟalum | iravuvaru vāṉaip pakalvaru keṉṟalum | pakaṉum iraviṉum payiṉṟuvaru keṉṟalum
The first two situations cited from the AV here resemble the content of the TNV poem closely, and the final one resembles the koḷu and the sources cited.
Cf. IAC30, p. 195: talaimakaṉai iraviṉkaṇṇum pakaliṉkaṇṇum vāraleṉṟu collutal
Cf. AV166.9: pakaṉum iraviṉum akalivaṇ eṉṟal
Cf. Kali24.14: yāmuyir vāḻu matukai yilēm
Cf. IAC30, p. 191: aḵtāmāṟu, emperumāṉ varumvaḻi iṟappavum iṉṉātu, nīruṭaittuk kalluṭaittu muḷḷuṭaittu ēṟṟuṭaittu iḻivuṭaitteṉak kavaṟal;
nam kātalar is a very well established phrase to refer to the hero, and am kātalar, which would be the reading of C1, occurs nowhere. Although one could make sense of it, it would be highly unlikely.

This final line bears some resemblance to Kali 24.14 in its meaning and context. Because of this similarity and the fact that uyir vāḻ-tal is normally preceded by a pronoun in the old akam corpus, UVC’s reading is chosen. One can also make sense of C1: ‘When our lover comes in the night, I am not strong, O friend! [How] will I live life?’.
Cf. KT88.2: ciṟukaṭ peruṅkaḷiṟu vayappuli tākkit
Cf. AN65.16–17: kōṭēn torutta | lāṟukaṭi koḷḷu maruñcuram
Cf. TK255.2–4: kuḻikaṭ kaḷiṟu verīiyari yāḷi kuḻīi vaḻaṅkāk | kaḻikaṭ ṭiraviṉ varalkaḻal kaitoḻu tēyirantēṉ | poḻikaṭ puyaliṉ mayiliṟ ṟuvaḷu mivaḷporuṭṭē ||

I do not see why UVC felt the need to emend C1 by adding peritu. Perhaps it was the infrequency of the form ūṟutu, which is not attested in the old corpus, and the relative frequency of an adapted version of a corrected KKms reading? If so, I would argue against both as grounds for emendation. The poem makes perfectly good sense without peritu, and the addition is not necessary for the metre. Though ūṟutu is not found in the old corpus, it is a grammatically sound form – a standard pronominal noun in the neuter singular. There are no compelling parallels I have found for this phrase and without one, I hesitate to emend on the strength of KKms. The readings found there are regularly corrupt, or at least markedly different from those transmitted by C1.

Cf. AN122.4–10 (IAC30, p. 190–191): valluraik kaṭuñco laṉṉai tuñcāḷ | piṇiko ḷaruñciṟai yaṉṉai tuñciṟ | ṟuñcāk kaṇṇar kāvalar kaṭukuva | rilaṅkuvē liḷaiyar tuñciṉ vaiyeyiṟṟu | valañcurit tōkāi ñāḷi makiḻu | maravavāy ñamali makiḻātu maṭiyiṟ | pakaluru vuṟaḻnilavuk kāṉṟu
Cf. PK219.2–3 (IAC30, p. 189): maṭantaiyic cēyiḻaiyā | ṭāyun tuyiṉmaṟan tāḷ
Cf. PK220.3–4 (IAC30, p. 190): ūrun tuyiṉṟiṭaṅ kāvalarō ṭaṉṉai yuḷḷuṟuttel | lārun tuyiliṉun tuñcā ñamali yaraiyiruḷē ||
Cf. PK221.4 (IAC30, p. 190): tuñcā tiraviv viyaṉakarē ||
Cf. PK222.3–4 (IAC30, p. 190): vaḷarnakar kākkumvai vēliḷaiñar | tuṭikkaṇ ṇiraṇṭuṅkaṅ kuṟṟalai yoṉṟun tuyiṉṟilavē ||
Cf. PK223.4 (IAC30, p. 190): niṉṟu vicumpiṟ pakalpōl viriyu nilāmatiyē ||
Cf. IAC30, p. 189: ‘ciṟaikāval’ eṉpatu, tāytuñcāmai nāytuñcāmai ūrtuñcāmai kāvalarkaṭukutal nilavu veḷippaṭutal tōḻikuraṟkāṭṭal eṉavivai.
Cf. TK175: iṉṉaṟa vārpoḻiṟ ṟillai nakariṟai cīrviḻaviṟ | paṉṉiṟa mālait tokaipaka lāmpal viḷakkiruḷiṉ | tuṉṉaṟa vuykkumil lōrun tuyiluṟ ṟuṟaivarmikka | koṉṉiṟa vēloṭu vantiṭiṉ ñāḷi kuraitarumē ||
Cf. AV161: tāyum nāyum ūruntuñ cāmai | kāvalar kaṭukutal nilavuveḷip paṭutal | kūkai kuḻaṟutal kōḻikuraṟ kāṭṭuta | lākiya ēḻum allukkuṟit talaivaṉ | varuntoḻiṟ karumai poruntuta luriya ||

The AV categorises this situation slightly differently, grouping it under the wider topic of the ‘hero’s difficulty in coming’. In practice though, AV cūttiram seems to either be based upon the AN poem cited above, or both it and the AN poem draw from a very well-established set of obstacles for the hero to overcome.
Cf. PK233.2–4 (IAC30, p. 194): pakaliṭanī | varavu makiḻntila ṭaiyalvey yōṉpōy malaimaṟainta | viravum varaveṉṉa vūṉameṉ ṟāyiṉa tiṉṉaruḷē ||
Cf. PK235.3–4 (IAC30, p. 194): pañcā rakalalkul pāṟpakal vantāṟ paḻiperitām | mañcār cilampa varaveṉṉa vūṉa mayaṅkiruḷē ||

Cf. AN118.5–10 (IAC30, p. 195): iyaṉmuru koppiṉai vayanāy piṟpaṭap | pakalvariṟ kavvai yañcutu mikalko | virumpiṭi kaṉṟoṭu viraīi kayavāyp | peruṅkai yāṉai kōṭpiḻait tarīiya | vaṭupuli vaḻaṅku māṟiru ṇaṭunāṭ | ṭaṉiyai varuta lataṉiṉu mañcutum
Cf. TK261.3–4: puri meṉkuḻa vāṭiṟat taiyameyyē | paḻiyām pakalvari ṉīyira vētum payaṉillaiyē ||

My assumption is that UVC emended here to retain etukai and because ira variṉ (‘if [you] come at night’) makes for a more natural counterpart to pakal variṉ (‘if [you] come in the day’) in line one. The reading is attested in KKms. I would argue that this departure from C1 is unnecessary. iruḷ variṉ (‘if [you] come in the dark’) makes good sense, and I think it much more likely that a scribe would have modified this original reading to ira variṉ. For it to have gone the other way would require a mistake that moved the poem away from etukai and the more natural pairing of pakal and ira, so C1 is the lectio difficilior. One could argue that etukai could be reasonably expected here as it would require little from the poet to accommodate it, but I find that speculative and insufficient to justify departing from C1. Further supporting this edition’s reading is line four of TNV 18, where we find the phrase iruḷ vara(l) vēṇṭal.
Cf. KT246.3–5: pāṉāṭ ṭaṉittōr | tērvantu peyarnta teṉpa vataṟkoṇ | ṭōru malaikku maṉṉai piṟarum
Cf. AN20.12–16: aṉṉai | kaṭikoṇ ṭaṉaḷē tōḻi peruntuṟai | yellaiyu miravu meṉṉātu kalleṉa | valava ṉāynta vaṇpari | nilavumaṇaṟ koṭkumōr tēruṇ ṭeṉavē ||
Cf. NA191.6–8: ellivan taṉṟō tēreṉac colli | yalareḻun taṉṟiv vūrē palaruḷu | meṉṉōk kiṉarē yaṉṉai

Cf. PK240 (IAC30, p. 197): aṉṉāy neruna ṉikaḻntatu kēḷayal vēntiṟaiñcum | poṉṉār kaḻaṉeṭu māṟaṉ kumariyam pūmpoḻilvāy | miṉṉār maṇineṭun tērkaṅkul vantoṉṟu mīṇṭatuṇṭā | leṉṉā mukañcivan temmaiyu nōkkiṉa ḷemmaṉaiyē ||
Cf. IAC30, p. 198: nerunal, aṉṉai nīṅkaḷ viḷaiyāṭuṅ kāṉaliṭattu oru tērvantu pōyiṟṟeṉa muṉintu eṉṉaiyum nōkkippōyiṉāḷ iṉṉatu karutiyeṉpatu aṟiyēṉeṉṉum.
Cf. TK256.2–4: malleḻiṟ kāṉa laraiyiraviṉ | aṇṇaṉ maṇineṭun tērvanta tuṇṭā meṉacciṟitu | kaṇṇuñ civantaṉṉai yeṉṉaiyu nōkkiṉaḷ kārmayilē ||

Cf. PK241 (IAC30, p. 198): paṇṇivar collikaṇ ṭāṭeṉṉaṉ pāḻip pakaitaṇitta | maṇṇivar cīrmaṉṉaṉ vāṇeṭu māṟaṉ malayameṉṉum | viṇṇivar kuṉṟat taruviceṉ ṟāṭiyor vēṅkaiyiṉkīḻk | kaṇṇivar kātaṟ piṭiyoṭu niṉṟa karuṅkaḷiṟē ||

Cf. TK257: vāṉṟōy poḻileḻiṉ māṅkaṉi mantiyiṉ vāykkaṭuvaṉ | tēṉṟōyt tarutti makiḻvakaṇ ṭāṭiru nīṇmuṭimēl | mīṉṟōy puṉaṟpeṇṇai vaittuṭai yāḷaiyu mēṉivattāṉ | vāṉṟōy matiṟṟillai mānakar pōlum varivaḷaiyē ||
The TK poem replaces elephants with monkeys but is otherwise similar.
Cf. TK135.1–2: vaḻiyu matuvaṉṉai yeṉṉiṉ makiḻumvan tentaiyuniṉ | moḻiyiṉ vaḻiniṟkuñ cuṟṟamuṉ ṉēvayam

One can see that the TK has a slightly different organisation from the TNV. The idea in many earlier poems in the TK, where the confidante refuses the hero’s requests to come for a tryst, is that the hero ought to marry the heroine.
Cf. TK251.2–4: vāṉakañcēr | arampaiyar tammiṭa mōvaṉṟi vēḻatti ṉeṉpunaṭṭa | kurampaiyar tammiṭa mōviṭan tōṉṟumik kuṉṟiṭattē ||

In terms of both meaning and syntax, C1 and Cām are similar: they are neuter singular participial nouns that mean something like ‘to realise/understand’. UVC seems to have edited on the strength of the KK, but that text is regularly corrupt, so I don’t consider it strong enough grounds for emendation without a compelling parallel, which I have not found. There is one Caṅkam collocation of yān teḷi-tal in AN 220.22, but it is used in a different context. Another reason to suspect the KK readings is that there was clearly some corruption in this poem. The subjects of the two clauses in the poem should be the same, and no witness reports anything but a first-person plural for the final phrase, matittaṉṟō vilamē, which precludes the possibility of the KK reading, yāṉ, in line one.

This TK poem is almost a precursor in the sequence to the poem in the TNV. It asks the question whether the heroine’s resting place is that of the gods, whereas in the TNV the hero has confirmed that he now knows that she is human like him and therefore approachable for marriage.
